headline: A structured pipeline cut false positive grading of research level mathematical proofs, but generality remains untested
summary: The Ramanujan Challenge authors report an AI-assisted workflow for reviewing research-level mathematical submissions in natural language, computer algebra and Lean. It executes submitted Python under a fixed environment, has separate agents summarize the proof and code, compares those summaries, then presents the result to a human reviewer. Against one-shot Claude Opus 5 judgments on the same challenge set, the authors report that false 'Correct' verdicts fell from 23.4% to 5.8% for 137 natural-language proofs and from 38.3% to 3.3% for 120 CAS/Lean artifacts. Agreement with one human evaluator rose from 65.7% to 66.4% for proofs and from 45.8% to 58.3% for code. The paper says each artifact was reviewed by one human without cross-checking; participants self-selected and reported their tools. These are one paper's results, not independent confirmation of generality or reduced expert workload.
